title: The Rig Split
primary_metric: blended barrels produced per rig-day, across both basins, for the remainder of the quarter

options.A: The Basin Shift — move 2 rigs off the Permian leases into the Bakken, paying the relocation-downtime cost and disrupting the most experienced crew, to chase the Bakken's higher per-rig productivity for the rest of the quarter
options.B: Hold the Line — keep the current allocation, no relocation downtime and no crew disruption, but the Permian rigs keep producing at their lower barrels-per-rig-day rate for the rest of the quarter

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4

deliverables.text: A system of equations, set up and written in matrix form, for the Basin Shift (Option A): define the three unknowns (Permian-producing rig-days, Bakken-producing rig-days, idle relocation rig-days), write the three governing linear equations, express as a coefficient matrix times a variable vector equal to a constant vector, and state the coefficient matrix's dimensions.

Solve the Option A system via a matrix method (Gaussian elimination or inverse matrix), including computing the coefficient matrix's determinant by row expansion (showing each 2x2 minor determinant used), verifying the solution by matrix multiplication, and (if using the inverse method) showing the coefficient matrix times its inverse yields the identity matrix.
Set up and solve Hold the Line (Option B)'s own system the same way, and address whether Option B's coefficient matrix is the same one used for Option A.

A blended-productivity comparison table: using the solved rig-day values from D2/D3 and Appendix D's real per-basin productivity rates, compute total barrels and blended barrels-per-rig-day for each option, and the percent difference between them.

A recommendation memo defended with D4's numbers and Appendix A/E's relocation-downtime figure, including a sensitivity check on how many fewer downtime days would flip the recommendation, and an explicit treatment of the crew-disruption cost from Background.

balance.argument_a: The Bakken genuinely out-produces the Permian on a real, sourced per-rig basis -- 1,747 vs. 1,400 barrels/day (S1, S2), a real ~24.8% per-rig-day productivity edge. Even after paying the full 14-day relocation-downtime cost (MA3, anchored to a real 1-4 week out-of-region range, S4) on both moved rigs, the Basin Shift still delivers 706,364 total barrels against Hold the Line's 713,640 -- decisively close, and the qualitative case for A only strengthens if the real downtime turns out shorter than 14 days (the breakeven point is 11.92 days -- see margin_note), which is well within the real cited range.
balance.argument_b: Hold the Line keeps every one of the 8 rigs producing every single day of the 60 remaining days in the quarter -- zero idle rig-days, zero lost production, and zero disruption to the most experienced crew on the company's original leases (a real cost Background names explicitly and that never enters the barrels-per-rig-day number at all). On the case's own stated 14-day downtime assumption, Hold the Line wins the blended metric outright: 713,640 vs. 706,364 total barrels, a margin of about 1.02%.
balance.margin_basis: For each option, solve the 3-variable/3-equation rig-day system (Permian-producing rig-days x, Bakken-producing rig-days y, idle rig-days z) via matrix methods, then compute blended barrels-per-rig-day = (1400*x + 1747*y) / (fixed total rig-day budget of 480). Compare the two options' blended rates; margin_pct is the percent by which the winner beats the loser.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-research). Fixed inputs: R=8 rigs (MA1), D=60 remaining days (MA2), L=14 relocation-downtime days per moved rig (MA3), k=2 rigs moved (given), rP=1400 bbl/day/rig (S1), rB=1747 bbl/day/rig (S2). Total rig-day budget = R*D = 480 for both options (fixed). OPTION A (Basin Shift): x = (P-k)*D = (6-2)*60 = 240 Permian rig-days; z = k*L = 2*14 = 28 idle rig-days; y = 480 - 240 - 28 = 212 Bakken rig-days. Barrels_A = 1400*240 + 1747*212 = 336,000 + 370,364 = 706,364. Blended_A = 706,364 / 480 = 1,471.59 bbl/rig-day. OPTION B (Hold the Line): x = P*D = 6*60 = 360 Permian rig-days; z = 0; y = 480 - 360 - 0 = 120 Bakken rig-days. Barrels_B = 1400*360 + 1747*120 = 504,000 + 209,640 = 713,640. Blended_B = 713,640 / 480 = 1,486.75 bbl/rig-day. WINNER: Option B, Hold the Line. margin_pct = (1486.75 - 1471.59) / 1486.75 * 100 = 1.02%. This is a genuinely razor-thin margin, comfortably inside SPEC §2's ~20% cap -- no retune needed. Breakeven check: solving (D-L)*rB = D*rP for L gives the relocation-downtime day count at which the two options tie exactly: L* = D*(1 - rP/rB) = 60*(1 - 1400/1747) = 60*0.198627 = 11.92 days. The case's stated MA3 value (14 days) sits only about 2.08 days above that breakeven -- i.e., the recommendation flips on a change of roughly 2 days in the relocation-downtime assumption, a real and honestly narrow sensitivity finding, not an artifact. See sensitivity_model.py.
balance.structural_notes: Neither option is structurally free: Option A pays a real, sourced downtime cost (28 idle rig-days) and a real, disclosed crew-disruption cost that never enters the metric; Option B pays an opportunity cost (forgoing the Bakken's real per-rig productivity edge for the whole 46 productive days those 2 rigs would otherwise have run in the Bakken). Primary metric exists and is computed for both options. Dilemma is not a foregone conclusion -- the numeric winner (Option B) is decided by a margin under 2 percentage points, and flips under a plausible ~2-day change to the case's single most sensitive Modeling Assumption (MA3).

modeling_assumptions.claim: Torchline's total fleet and its Permian/Bakken split
modeling_assumptions.basis: Stated in-scenario, sized to fit "mid-size independent operator" well below either basin's real total rig count (Appendix F: Permian 242, Williston 29, both Baker Hughes, S5).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Scales both options' totals but does not change which option wins -- the margin comes from the ratio between relocation downtime and the basin productivity gap, not fleet size.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Remaining days left in the current quarter, as of case launch
modeling_assumptions.basis: Stated in-scenario -- matches a mid-quarter checkpoint review, not the literal last day of the quarter.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: MEDIUM -- a longer remaining-quarter window gives the moved rigs more productive days to recoup the fixed 14-day downtime cost, so a large enough increase (confirmed by sensitivity_model.py: +25% and +50%, i.e. 75+ remaining days) flips the winner to Option A. At the stated 60-day value and below, Option B wins. Not the case's primary sensitivity lever (see MA3), but not fully inert either.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Anchored to Appendix E's real, cited 1-4-week range for an out-of-region rig move (S4, MineralView) -- 14 days sits in the lower-middle of that real range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- the single most dilemma-relevant modeling choice in the case. Breakeven downtime is 11.92 days (see balance.margin_note); the stated 14-day value sits only ~2.08 days above that breakeven, so a small, plausible change to this one assumption flips the recommendation.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (1.02%) is a genuinely close, razor-thin margin computed entirely from real EIA productivity data (S1, S2) plus the case's three stated Modeling Assumptions (MA1-MA3). MA3 (relocation downtime, 14 days) is by far the most load-bearing: the breakeven downtime is 11.92 days, so the recommendation flips under roughly a 2-day change -- well within the real cited 1-4-week range (S4) this assumption is anchored to. MA1 (fleet size and Permian/Bakken split) does not flip the winner across a +-50% sweep. MA2 (remaining quarter days) does NOT flip the winner within a -50%/-25% sweep, but DOES flip it at +25% and +50% (i.e. 75+ remaining days) -- a longer remaining window gives moved rigs more time to recoup the fixed 14-day downtime cost. Confirmed by directly running sensitivity_model.py's probe-5 sweep, not just derived by hand. See sensitivity_model.py.

cohort_bands.note: The size the case was authored for. Socratic plan and Anchor timings run as written (45 minutes, all 4 anchors, twist, threaded deep conflict).

Anchors 2-3 combine into one pass; the twist still drops at the same relative point but only one deep-conflict thread runs (recommend the 'is the crew cost really outside the model' thread, since it has the sharpest values-payoff); total runtime shortens to roughly 30 minutes, content held constant.

No vote to take at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position instead. The facilitator plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands; 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse your recommendation, and why.'

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2 (60 days remaining in the quarter) is a stated in-scenario framing choice ('the night before Friday's quarterly review implies a mid-quarter checkpoint'), not a citable real figure. The case's base margin is only 1.03% by design (matching the SPEC-cited Robotics Engineering gold standard of an extremely close race) so almost any dial can flip a razor-thin margin -- MA3 (relocation downtime) is the dominant, explicitly disclosed driver; case.json's balance.margin_note documents the exact breakeven downtime value D5 asks students to derive.

MA3 is explicitly flagged 'the single most dilemma-relevant modeling choice in the case' in case.md, anchored to Appendix E's real cited 1-4-week out-of-region relocation range (S4). Case.md states outright: 'the case's real recommendation flips on a change of only a couple of days either side of 14' -- this exact flip is the case's designed mechanism (D5 asks students to compute the breakeven value themselves), not a hidden instability.
